archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (still a below-average team)
archetype.definition: A Calgary side whose 2-6-0 start and league-worst goal differential are inflated by a goaltending and finishing collapse, but whose underlying chance quality and last two seasons still point to a non-playoff team rather than a hidden contender.

report.headline: Bad, not this bad: a goaltending meltdown is masking a merely mediocre team
report.take:
Calgary sits 28th of 32 on the site, 2-6-0 and last in the league in Goal Diff / GP at -2.5. They have scored 17 and allowed 37 over eight games, and their 82-game pace is 41 standings points. That number will not hold. Almost everything driving it is the kind of percentage that swings hardest over eight games.

Start in net. The Flames' all-situations save percentage is .847, last in the league against a .893 average, and Goalies GSAx is -9.7, also last. Dustin Wolf owns most of that damage with an .834 save percentage and -8.0 GSAx in five starts. This is the same position that bailed the team out the last two years, at +16.7 GSAx in 2024-25 and +14.2 last season. Up front, the skaters are shooting 7.1%, 30th, against a league mark of 11.3%. Add the two together and you get an all-situations PDO of 91.8, dead last, with the 5-on-5 version at 91.7. No team stays there.

The numbers also hide that Calgary is not simply getting caved in. They are taking 30 shots a game, seventh in the league, and own 53% of 5-on-5 shot attempts, eighth. The special teams are both a bit better than league average. The catch is that the volume is not turning into quality: xGF % is 48.3%, 22nd, and they are giving up 29.5 shots a game, 28th. This is a team that has the puck a lot without generating better looks than it allows. It also looks a lot like last season's 77-point, 47% xGF club that finished 32nd in scoring.

Where this goes: the goals-against rate falls sharply once Wolf looks anything like his recent self, and the shooting percentage rises some. Even so, the finishing problem is chronic, since offense ranked 29th and 32nd the last two years, and the chance share is below water. Expect a steady climb out of the basement toward the bottom-ten tier, not a playoff push. A five-game losing streak to open the year, followed by 2-1 in the last three, is the first sign of that correction.

strengths.title: They are winning the shot-attempt battle
strengths.body: Calgary controls 53% of 5-on-5 shot attempts, eighth in the league, and puts 30 shots on goal a game, seventh. That is real territorial play rather than a fluke, and it is in line with the 51-52% attempt shares of the past few seasons. It is the main reason to believe the goal totals will improve once pucks start going in.

strengths.title: Special teams are holding up
strengths.body: The power play is converting at 21.1%, 12th, and the penalty kill is at 81.5%, 14th, both above the league averages. With even-strength goals so scarce, special teams have been one of the few phases not bleeding goals. The power play has also improved on last season's 16.2%, though eight games is a thin sample for either unit.

concerns.title: Goaltending has gone from asset to anchor
concerns.body: Calgary's goalies are last in GSAx at -9.7 and last in save percentage at .847, and the group grades an F. Wolf's -8.0 GSAx in five starts is the core of it, with Devin Cooley at -2.6 not providing relief. This should regress hard toward normal given the +14.2 team GSAx last season. Until it does, though, no amount of shot share keeps games close.

concerns.title: Possession without chance quality
concerns.body: Despite the 53% attempt share, Calgary's xGF % is only 48.3%, 22nd. They also allow 29.5 shots a game, 28th, and opposing centers are outproducing their norms against them, with this team ranked 31st in holding centers down. That is a structural defensive problem, not just bad goaltending, and it matches the sub-50% expected-goal shares of the last two seasons.

concerns.title: Finishing is a long-running problem
concerns.body: A 7.1% shooting rate, 30th, will rise, but this roster finished 32nd in scoring last year and 29th the year before. Joel Farabee leads the forwards in ice time and has no goals on 20 shots. The forward group grades D-, so a bounce in shooting luck lifts them toward mediocre, not toward a good offense.

trend.note: Calgary opened with a five-game losing streak, mostly by lopsided scores, then went 2-1. Over the last five games they have averaged 2.8 goals for and 4.2 against, with the differential improved by 1.1 goals a game on the season rate.

weekAhead.headline: Three at home: one heavyweight, two beatable mid-pack teams
weekAhead.body:
The week is all home games. It opens against Minnesota, fourth on the site at 6-2-1, with a top-five defense and an A- goaltending group stopping .922. That is the worst possible matchup for a Calgary team that cannot finish. Detroit (22nd) and Toronto (21st) follow, and both are winnable on paper. Detroit is shooting even worse than the Flames at 7.8% and ranks 28th in scoring. Toronto is being outchanced badly with a 44.4% xGF %.

A realistic target is two wins from three. That depends less on matchups than on whether the goaltending stops the bleeding. Calgary's shot volume should travel against Detroit and Toronto, both of which give up plenty of shots. Minnesota allows 22.7 shots a game and limits wingers better than almost anyone, so expect a low-event grind there.

keyMatchups.title: Calgary power play vs Detroit's kill
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's penalty kill is at 69%, 28th in the league, while Calgary converts 21.1% of its chances. In a game between two teams that struggle to score at even strength, drawing penalties may decide it. This is the clearest edge Calgary has all week.

keyMatchups.title: Minnesota's power play and goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Wild convert 32.1% of their power plays, second in the league, and their goalies are saving .922. Against a Calgary team saving .847, staying out of the box matters more than usual. Calgary's shot volume may run into a wall here.

keyMatchups.title: Calgary volume vs Toronto's leaky blue line
keyMatchups.body: Toronto allows 29.2 shots a game, 26th, posts a 44.4% xGF %, and its defense grades D-. That is the matchup where Calgary's attempt share should turn into real chances. The catch is Toronto's league-best 96.4% penalty kill, so the damage has to come at five-on-five.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net, and whether Calgary's team save percentage finally climbs off the league floor.

restOfSeason.body:
The 41-point pace is noise. A save percentage 46 points below the league average and a 91.8 PDO will not survive 74 more games, especially for a goaltending group that was well above expected the last two seasons. As the goals-against rate normalizes and the shooting percentage creeps up, Calgary should play much closer to .500 hockey than its first eight games suggest. I project roughly 66 to 78 points.

That ceiling is still well short of the playoffs. The parts that look sustainable, the shot-attempt share and decent special teams, coexist with a sub-50% expected-goal share, a D- forward group and a scoring problem that goes back years. The hole dug in October also leaves little margin. Expect a team that climbs into the mid-20s of the site's rankings, not one that contends in the Pacific.
